images.name: The trodden, marked road that takes its walker in
images.source: chain map: Orientation, Passage, and Breakdown > A. The Marked and Straight Route; Orientation, Passage, and Breakdown > C. Engulfing and Penetrating Passage; Orientation, Passage, and Breakdown > E. Disorientation, Forgetting, and the Stray; Devotional Dependence and Rule > C. Petition for Aid and Direction
images.scene: A desert route with waymarks standing along it and a clear middle course. Many feet have trodden its surface smooth. A guide gently shows the way and keeps the heading. The road is straight and takes its walker in as easily as a throat takes a morsel. Someone who leaves it wanders off the course and disappears into the waste.

members.role: waymarks (maʿālim al-ṭarīq, ʿalam as mountain or marker) standing along the route; creatures as marks that point the way
malak al-ṭarīq: the middle and main course of the road (minor)
the road surface: ṭarīq muʿabbad, a road made smooth and level by being walked
the guide who shows the road gently (bi-luṭf)
the heading and set direction of travel (hady as jiha, sīra, ṭarīqa)
the road itself
the road that takes its walker in (yastariṭu sālikahu), audible through the canonical sirāṭ reading
swallowing: the walker passes into the road with ease
the road's straightness and evenness
the road named after the people who walked it
the wanderer who leaves the course and loses the way
the one who goes missing, absorbed into the waste

images.containment: 'Guide us to the straight path' stays the plea for the right religious way. The Arabic also lays out a physical road: marked, trodden smooth by those who went before, taking its walker in, and left by a wanderer who is lost in the waste.
images.perceptible: It makes the path spatial and historical. The road already exists and has been walked: the verb of worship, naʿbudu, shares its root with the road made smooth by feet (muʿabbad). In 1:7 the road is identified by the people who walked it ('the road of those…'), not by a description. The sirāṭ reading hears a road that takes its walker in. Ḍalla also means to vanish into something. So the surah shows two ways of disappearing: into the road, carried along, or into the waste, lost.

interactions.how: The stray beast of I2 is the animal form of the wanderer who leaves this road. The lead animal (hādī) and the guide (hādī) share one word.
The walker on this road is the weak walker of I6, held up by supporters while moving forward.
The road is defined by favor ('those you favored'), and guidance onto it is asked for as a gently sent gift.
The ʿabd of 1:5 and the trodden road share one root. Serving and treading the road become one act of repeated going.

images.movement: It carries the turn from address (1:1–5) to petition (1:6–7). The servants who declared themselves in 1:5 ask to be set on a road that others have already made smooth by walking it.

images.name: The branded herd, its owner, its lead animal and the stray
images.source: chain map: Herd Formation, Wildlife, and Dispersal > A. Herd, Livestock, and the Stray Margin; Orientation, Passage, and Breakdown > B. The Visible Leader at the Front; Orientation, Passage, and Breakdown > E. Disorientation, Forgetting, and the Stray
images.scene: A herd of camels carries its owner's brand. It goes out from and returns to its owner's resting-place, following a lead animal at the front. One beast has strayed. It is left in a wasteland, and no one can tell who its owner is.

members.role: the brand (wasm, sima) by which an animal is known as someone's; documented alternative derivation of ism
the owner: rabb al-dābba, master of the beast
marabb al-ibil: the place where the camels stay
the animal that goes in front and the rest follow (minor)
the hādī: the front of the herd, the lead animal
the herd itself (naʿam, camels), heard beside ḍāllīn (minor)
the ḍālla: a beast left in a wasteland 'whose owner (rabb) is not known'
the thing gone from its owner, whose place cannot be found

images.containment: 'In the name of God' and 'those who go astray' keep their plain senses. Underneath, the surah also opens with the mark by which an owner's beast is known and closes with a beast that has lost all sign of its owner.
images.perceptible: The dictionary defines the ḍālla as the beast 'whose rabb is not known'. The word the surah uses for God in 1:2 is built into the definition of what it asks to be kept from in 1:7. So straying is relational, not only a wrong turn: it is losing one's tie to an owner who knows you. The surah is framed between the mark of belonging (bismi heard through wasm) and the unmarked stray.

interactions.how: The stray is the wanderer off the road, seen as livestock. The lead animal at the front is the guide.
Rabb and mālik as owner of animals match their role as master of servants. Both scenes rest on belonging to someone.
Ḍalla B003 (a loss gone from its owner) also sits in I5's vocabulary of claims left unsettled.

images.movement: It frames the whole surah: belonging announced at the start, the danger of becoming an ownerless stray named at the end. The petition in 1:6–7 asks to stay one of the owner's known herd.

images.name: The womb and the one who raises stage by stage
images.source: chain map: Household Continuity and Protected Belonging > A. Kinship, Fosterage, and Continuing Care; Household Continuity and Protected Belonging > B. Gestation, Recent Birth, and Postpartum Vulnerability; Benefaction, Welfare, and Praise > A. Compassionate Provision and Nurture
images.scene: A womb holds growing young. Kin are bound by the tie of the womb. A newly delivered mother stays home to nurse, and a caregiver takes charge of a child and raises it stage by stage until it is complete.

members.role: tenderness and kindness toward the one shown mercy
the womb as the house where offspring grows
the kinship tie that comes from the womb
the one who puts a thing right and completes it, raising it 'stage by stage' (tarbiya ḥālan fa-ḥālan)
the fosterer (rābb, rābba) who takes charge of the rabīb, the child in their care
the ewe that has just given birth and stays home for its milk (minor)
mercy named again, after the rabb
the womb heard again around the rabb

images.containment: 'The Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful' stays God's mercy. The Arabic keeps raḥim, the womb, audible inside it, and rabb keeps the one who raises a dependent step by step.
images.perceptible: In Turkish, rahmet has become an abstract pity or rain. Here mercy becomes bodily and connected to kin: the tenderness of a womb toward what grows inside it. Rabb is placed between two mentions of the mercy names (1:1, 1:3), so lordship is heard wrapped in womb-tenderness: an owner who also raises, stage by stage, over time.

interactions.how: It softens I4 from inside: the same rabb who owns also raises, and the mercy names come before the owner of the Day.
Womb-mercy is where the favor (niʿma) of 1:7 comes from.

images.movement: It sets the tone of the address before sovereignty and judgment arrive. The Lord met first is the one who raises and carries.

images.name: The master's household: owner, king and the owned one
images.source: chain map: Devotional Dependence and Rule > A. Worship and Obedient Submission; Devotional Dependence and Rule > B. Sovereignty, Ownership, and Service
images.scene: A household under a master who owns and a king who rules. Dominion is exercised and obedience given. The owned one steps forward and speaks in the first person: you alone we serve.

members.role: the owner and obeyed master (rabb al-dār)
the owner and possessor (mālik, canonical reading)
the king who rules (malik, mutawatir reading)
dominion and subjugation, the one held in service
obedience and submission
the ʿabd: the owned one, the opposite of free
worship as humble, submissive obedience

images.containment: 'Master of the Day of Judgment' and 'You alone we worship' keep their devotional sense. The Arabic also stages a household in which the owned ones speak directly to the one who owns them.
images.perceptible: In Turkish, ibadet has narrowed to ritual acts. Naʿbudu keeps the ʿabd, the whole person as someone's own. The two canonical readings keep owner (mālik) and king (malik) both alive in 1:4. The switch from third person (1:2–4) to 'You' (1:5) is the moment the owned ones stop speaking about the master and turn to face him.

interactions.how: The mercy names frame this ownership, so owning is heard alongside raising.
The owner is the owner of a Day when what is owed is settled. Dīn means both dominion and account.
Right after declaring themselves servants, the servants ask for support.
ʿAbd also names the road smoothed by treading. The servant's service becomes the walking of 1:6.

images.movement: It is the hinge of the surah. Descriptions of the Lord (1:2–4) turn into the servants' direct speech (1:5), which makes the petition of 1:6–7 possible.

images.name: The day when what is owed is settled
images.source: chain map: Time, Measure, and Final Reckoning > C. The Momentous Day of Rising and Account; Property, Measure, and Legitimate Transfer > A. Credit, Price, and Livestock Property; Property, Measure, and Legitimate Transfer > B. Replacement, Indemnity, and Redress; Conflict, Anger, and Defensive Order > B. Anger, Mourning, Vengeance, and Redress
images.scene: A debt runs to a fixed term, and a momentous day arrives when the term falls due. The one who owns that day settles every account and gives each their due. Claims are answered: blood-money in place of retaliation, anger that rises to demand redress, and blood that goes unavenged.

members.role: the owner of the day of settlement
the momentous day, the event that comes down
reckoning, recompense and judgment
a debt, and sale to a fixed term (ajal)
ghayr as blood-money taken in place of retaliation (minor)
anger that rises and seeks redress
what is gone without redress: blood that 'goes' unavenged (minor)

images.containment: 'The Day of Judgment' stays the Day of Judgment. Dīn also holds debt and its due term, so the Day is heard as the day when everything owed is settled.
images.perceptible: Din in Turkish means 'religion'. Here it becomes time and money: an account running toward a fixed day. That makes the Day a due date rather than an abstraction. In 1:7 three consecutive words (ghayr, maghḍūb, ḍāllīn) also belong to the vocabulary of claims and redress, a faint echo that the end of the surah stands under the Day named in 1:4.

interactions.how: The master who owns the servants also owns the day their accounts are settled.
Favor received (niʿma) is what the account is reckoned against. Praise comes first as acknowledgment of what is owed.
Ḍalla B003, loss without redress, is shared with the stray scene.

images.movement: It gives the address its gravity just before the turn to 'You'. The servants speak knowing a settling day lies ahead. The 1:7 members are left for a light touch at most (that ayah's slots go to I1, I2, I7).

images.name: The weak walker held up between supporters
images.source: chain map: Devotional Dependence and Rule > C. Petition for Aid and Direction; Orientation, Passage, and Breakdown > D. Halted, Supported, and Recovered Movement; Benefaction, Welfare, and Praise > B. Patronage, Support, and Claimed Recognition
images.scene: A traveler's mount has broken down. Too weak to walk alone, the traveler goes forward leaning on two people, swaying, held up by them. Something they rest on keeps them standing.

members.role: the breakdown: aʿbada bihi, when a traveler's mount gives out and leaves them stranded (minor, activated by nastaʿīn beside it)
seeking help and backing (istiʿāna)
yuhādā bayna ithnayn: walking while leaning on two supporters out of weakness
qiwām: the support that keeps a thing standing

images.containment: 'You alone we ask for help; guide us' keeps its plain sense. The same words can also carry the posture of a weak walker going forward while leaning on support.
images.perceptible: It makes the petition bodily. Asking for help (1:5) and asking for guidance (1:6) come one after the other. The root of ihdinā also names walking while leaning on others, so guidance is heard not only as being shown the way but as being held up while walking it.

interactions.how: The weak walker is on I1's road. The guide is also the support.
The servants who declared service now admit they cannot walk alone.

images.movement: It joins the two halves of 1:5 to 1:6: declared dependence becomes a moving posture.

images.name: Gift gently sent, favor received, praise returned
images.source: chain map: Benefaction, Welfare, and Praise > A. Compassionate Provision and Nurture; Benefaction, Welfare, and Praise > B. Patronage, Support, and Claimed Recognition; Benefaction, Welfare, and Praise > C. Knowing and Articulating the Praiseworthy; Property, Measure, and Legitimate Transfer > C. Reciprocal Gift and Beneficent Transfer
images.scene: A giver gently sends gifts to someone they hold dear and puts the recipient in a good, easy state. The recipient answers with praise and thanks.

members.role: praise and thanks answering a favor
rubā: favor and kindness (minor)
the hadiyya: a gentle gift sent to someone held in affection
guidance given gently (bi-luṭf)
the favor bestowed: good state and good life (niʿma)
softness and ease of life (minor)

images.containment: 'Guide us' stays a request for guidance. Its root also names the gentle gift (hadiyya), and the favored are those who received a gift and a good state.
images.perceptible: A Turkish reader already has hidayet and hediye without knowing they are one root. Heard together, guidance becomes something sent gently to someone loved. The surah opens with the thanks (ḥamd) and closes by naming the favor (anʿamta), so praise comes first and the favor is named only at the end.

interactions.how: The road is identified by favor: it is the road of the favored.
The favor grows out of womb-mercy.
Praise acknowledges what has been received before the Day of accounts.

images.movement: It gives the surah its outer frame: thanks at 1:2, the gift asked for at 1:6, the favor named at 1:7.

concepts.concept: The womb's tenderness: closeness that holds, carries and feeds what grows inside it, extending outward into kinship
Taking charge of something and staying by it until it is complete: owning, raising stage by stage, fostering, remaining in place
A mark that makes a thing known: knowing, the waymark, and creation as a mark pointing to its maker
The name as what rises into view and makes something known (height, a figure seen from afar, good repute), with و س م (the brand) as the documented alternative derivation
A binding relation of owing between a superior and a dependent: obedience, dominion, debt, reckoning, settled habit
Being made low and smooth through use: the owned one, humble service, the road smoothed by treading, the tarred and tamed camel
Leading or sending something gently to where it belongs: guiding, the heading, the lead at the front, the gift, the bride conveyed, the offering, walking held up by others
Passing through without obstruction: the straight road, swallowing easily, the blade that goes through its stroke
Standing upright: an erect body, a straight road, the mainstay that holds something up
Going missing from where one should be known: straying from the course, vanishing into something, being lost to an owner, slipping from memory, the ownerless stray
A firm hold that keeps a thing together: firm kneading, possession, kingship, the mainstay
Softness and good condition: favor, ease of life, a place that suits one

movement: The surah moves from being named and marked (1:1, bismi, which can also be heard as wasm, the owner's brand) to an owner who raises (rabb) wrapped on both sides in womb-mercy (1:1–3). It then reaches the owner and king of a Day on which what is owed is settled (1:4). At 1:5 the owned ones stop speaking about the master and speak to him, declaring service and leaning on him for help. From that posture they ask to be led, held up and gifted onto a road already trodden smooth by the favored. That road takes its walker in (1:6–7). Their thanks were given at the start, and they ask not to become the stray beast in the waste whose owner no one knows. The surah's arc runs from the mark of belonging to the danger of being an unmarked stray, with praise answering a favor it only names at the end.

plan.note: Ism can also be heard from wasm, the mark by which an owner's animal is known. Raḥmān and raḥīm keep raḥim, the womb, audible under the flattened Turkish 'rahmet'.
Ḥamd is thanks for favors not yet named. Rabb is the owner and master (rabb al-dābba) and also the one who raises stage by stage. ʿĀlamīn are creatures as marks and waymarks pointing to their maker.
Mercy named again after rabb wraps lordship in womb-tenderness: the owner of 1:2 is also the one who carries and raises.
Both canonical readings keep owner (mālik) and king (malik) alive. Dīn holds obedience, dominion, account and debt, so the Day is a due date when what is owed is settled.
The owned ones turn to face their master. Naʿbudu keeps the whole person as ʿabd, beyond Turkish 'ibadet'. Nastaʿīn is the servant admitting they cannot walk alone.

Ihdinā is one root with hidayet and hediye: guidance sent gently like a gift, and walking held up between supporters. Ṣirāṭ/sirāṭ is a road that takes its walker in. Mustaqīm is upright. Naʿbudu's road smoothed by treading surfaces here.

The road is named by those who walked it and were favored, and the niʿma finally answers the ḥamd of 1:2. Ḍāllīn is the one who wanders off and vanishes into the waste, the stray beast 'whose rabb is not known', which closes the arc begun by the mark of 1:1.

chains_set_aside.title: Declared Identity and Public Presence > B. Assent, Certification, and Qualification
chains_set_aside.why: Naʿam as 'yes', tadyīn, ghayr as exception, and rubba as a particle are grammatical and logical senses with no scene to make perceptible here.

chains_set_aside.title: Declared Identity and Public Presence > C. Reputation and Poetic Exchange
chains_set_aside.why: Exchanging praise and satire in verse and spreading repute do not enter the surah's scene. Ism as elevation is kept in the concepts instead.

chains_set_aside.title: Declared Identity and Public Presence > D. The Reputed Captain's Ceremonial Bearing
chains_set_aside.why: Built from isolated minor branches (chief sailor, perfume vessel) that no word here activates.

chains_set_aside.title: Orientation, Passage, and Breakdown > B. The Visible Leader at the Front
chains_set_aside.why: Absorbed into I2 (the lead animal hādī and malak). As a separate procession it adds nothing.

chains_set_aside.title: Time, Measure, and Final Reckoning > A. Daylight, Zenith, and Celestial Marking
chains_set_aside.why: Zenith (qiyām al-ẓahīra) and the constellation senses have no activator. The Day of 1:4 is carried by I5 as a momentous day and a due term.

chains_set_aside.title: Time, Measure, and Final Reckoning > B. Duration, Pace, and Praised Attainment
chains_set_aside.why: Pace and attainment branches are scattered, with no shared scene and no payoff for the plain reading.

chains_set_aside.title: Property, Measure, and Legitimate Transfer > D. Consecrated Offering
chains_set_aside.why: Hady as an offering to the sanctuary is not activated by anything in the surah. The gift facet of the root is carried by I7.

chains_set_aside.title: Household Continuity and Protected Belonging > C. Marriage and Bride-Conveyance
chains_set_aside.why: Imlāk and the bride led to her husband pair only mechanically. Its gentle-conveyance facet is covered by I7 and the ه د ي concept.

chains_set_aside.title: Household Continuity and Protected Belonging > D. Covenant, Refuge, and Legal Protection
chains_set_aside.why: The rabāba pact and the protected client have no activator in the window.

chains_set_aside.title: Household Continuity and Protected Belonging > E. Protective Jealousy and Household Defense
chains_set_aside.why: Ghayra as jealousy for one's household comes from a different vocalization and nothing here calls for it.

chains_set_aside.title: Herd Formation, Wildlife, and Dispersal > B. Hunt, Flight, and Scattered Routes
chains_set_aside.why: Hunting and scattering routes are not activated. The one leaving the road is carried by I1 and I2.

chains_set_aside.title: Herd Formation, Wildlife, and Dispersal > C. Wildlife Generation and Exposure
chains_set_aside.why: Hyena, falcon and ostrich are lexical homonyms with no activator.

chains_set_aside.title: Habitation, Water, and the Living Landscape (A, B, C)
chains_set_aside.why: Settlement, water and rain-cloud branches are generous scene-map matches that no neighbouring word activates, so they have nothing to make perceptible here.

chains_set_aside.title: Structural Support and Working Materials (A, B, C)
chains_set_aside.why: Well gear, coating and cohesion are material homonyms. Only qiwām/milāk as mainstay survives, inside I6 and the concepts.

chains_set_aside.title: Bodily Integrity, Posture, and Injury (A, B, C, D)
chains_set_aside.why: Lesions, lip clefts, eye swellings and pubic hair are homonymous branches with no activation. Upright standing is kept in the ق و م concept.

chains_set_aside.title: Conflict, Anger, and Defensive Order > A. Rivalry, Resistance, and Repeated War
chains_set_aside.why: Rivalry and repeated war are not activated. Nastaʿīn is heard as backing, not battle.

chains_set_aside.title: Conflict, Anger, and Defensive Order > C. Rout and Collective Dispersal
chains_set_aside.why: The ostrich's flight and the scattered groups have no activator.

chains_set_aside.title: Conflict, Anger, and Defensive Order > D. Hardness, Shielding, and the Cutting Edge
chains_set_aside.why: The rock, the shield-hide and the sword join no scene with a payoff. The blade is kept only in the ص ر ط concept.

chains_set_aside.title: S1. The Divinatory Arrow Vessel
chains_set_aside.why: A single homonym of ر ب ب that nothing here activates.

other_activations: 1:1:1 س م و B001/B002: the name as what rises and is seen from afar (the Basran derivation), activated by the waymark and heading vocabulary later in the surah. Kept in the concept, not an image.
1:1:2 و ل ه~alt B001: walah, bewildered longing, heard in the alternative derivation of the divine name; faintly answered by the lostness of ḍāllīn.
1:1:4 ر ح م B004: the womb that aches after birth, activated by the womb branch B003. The tenderness that costs.
1:2:1 ح م د B005: taḥammud, seeking praise for one's favors, activated by anʿamta. Here praise is given before the favor is named.
1:2:1 ح م د B004: ḥamādāk, the praiseworthy utmost end, activated by the road's destination in 1:6–7.
1:5:2 ع ب د B006: muʿabbad as the honored and served one, activated by the master scene. The root names both server and served.
1:5:2 ع ب د B010: ʿabādīd, groups and roads scattering in every direction, activated by ḍāllīn as the opposite of one straight road.
1:5:2 ع ب د B008: ʿabad as indignation and grief, activated by maghḍūb in 1:7.
1:6:1 ه د ي B006 with 1:4:1 م ل ك B004: the bride conveyed to her husband and the marriage contract, a mechanical pair.
1:6:1 ه د ي B010: hady as calm, composed gait, unlike the hurry of someone fleeing, activated by the road and the manner of walking it.
1:6:2 ص ر ط B003: the blade that goes through its stroke, gathered into the ص ر ط concept of unobstructed passage.
1:6:3 ق و م B016: an animal that stands still, exhausted and unable to go on, activated by the broken-down mount of I6 and in tension with mustaqīm.
1:7:3 ن ع م B011: a land that suits one so one stays there, activated by the road's destination.
1:7:3 ن ع م B013: the cool, gladdened eye (qurrat al-ʿayn), activated by favor.
1:7:6 غ ض ب B004/B008: the hard rock and the stiff hide, a hardness beneath anger with no scene to join.
1:7:9 ض ل ل B004: slipping from memory, activated by ʿilm (knowing) in ʿālamīn.
